payload.throughline: Treat capacitance as a geometry-and-material property, then state what is held fixed before predicting charge, voltage, energy, network, or dielectric behavior.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: compare one geometric change. Leaving the response blank records an abstention and cannot satisfy an exit.

Goal: predict how ideal parallel-plate capacitance changes with plate overlap area and separation. The packet declares no hard prerequisite, so the proportional model is introduced before any consequential item.
For ideal parallel plates, C = εA/d. At fixed material and separation, a larger overlapping plate area gives proportionally larger capacitance.
At fixed material and area, greater plate separation gives smaller capacitance. The permittivity ε represents the intervening material.
Capacitance describes how much charge is stored per volt: C = Q/V. For unchanged geometry and material, adding charge also raises voltage; it does not redefine C.
Mental model: wider electrical “storage frontage” increases C; a larger gap weakens the plate coupling and decreases C. Read A and d before reading Q or V.

Think aloud: capacitor B has twice the overlap area and three times the separation of capacitor A. The area contributes a factor of 2 and separation contributes a factor of 1/3, so CB/CA = 2/3. Charge labels are irrelevant unless geometry or material also changes.
Worked example: a capacitor keeps the same material and plate area while separation changes from d to d/2. Because d is in the denominator, the new capacitance is 2C.
A second capacitor doubles both area and separation. The two factors cancel, so its capacitance is unchanged.
Guided practice: write the area factor in the numerator and the separation factor in the denominator before combining them.
Less support: compare two labelled plate diagrams using only “area helps; distance opposes.”
On your own: predict a geometry ratio without a displayed equation scaffold.

Boundary: doubling stored charge on unchanged plates does not double capacitance. It doubles voltage because Q = CV while C remains fixed by geometry and material. The ideal relation also assumes edge effects are neglected.
Near exit: calculate a fresh capacitance ratio from simultaneous area and separation changes.
Changed-task exit: infer the geometry change that explains a measured charge increase at the same applied voltage.
Repair the ratio function: write Cnew/Cold = (Anew/Aold)(dold/dnew). Separation reverses because it is in the denominator.
Fresh near re-entry: combine a new area factor with a new separation factor; no exposed numbers or options recur.
Repair the evidence-to-geometry function: at equal voltage, Q follows C. Translate the measured charge ratio into a capacitance ratio before selecting the geometry.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: use a different fixed-voltage observation to infer a plate change without reusing the prior answer.
Recap: ideal parallel-plate capacitance follows εA/d. Increase overlap area to raise C, increase separation to lower C, and do not confuse stored charge with capacitance.
Starting check: identify one direct Q–V relationship. A blank response is a nonconsequential abstention.

Goal: compare capacitor charge and stored energy by first identifying capacitance and then stating whether voltage or charge is held fixed. No hard prerequisite handoff is declared, so every equation used is developed here.
Charge and voltage obey Q = CV. For a fixed capacitor, doubling voltage doubles stored charge.
Stored energy can be written U = 1/2 CV², U = 1/2 QV, or U = Q²/(2C). These are equivalent descriptions of the same stored energy.
Choose the form that keeps the controlled quantity visible. At fixed C, voltage changes produce a squared energy change. At fixed Q, increasing C lowers energy.
Mental model: C sets the charge-per-volt capacity; Q tracks V linearly for fixed C, while energy measures the accumulated work and therefore carries a square in V.
Think aloud: the same capacitor moves from V to 3V. Q follows V, so Q becomes 3Q. Using U = 1/2 CV², energy becomes 9U. I do not assume the same factor for Q and U.
Worked example: a 2 μF capacitor at 3 V stores Q = CV = 6 μC. Its energy is 1/2(2 μF)(3 V)² = 9 μJ.
If voltage doubles on the same capacitor, charge doubles and energy quadruples.
Guided practice: circle the held quantity, select the equation that keeps it explicit, and then compare factors before substituting units.
Less support: distinguish a linear charge change from a squared energy change.
On your own: compare energy using a fresh capacitance or voltage ratio.

Boundary: U is not generally QV; the stored energy is 1/2 QV because voltage rises from zero as charge is accumulated. Also, changing C at fixed V is not the same administration as changing C at fixed Q.
Near exit: calculate charge and energy factors for the same capacitor after a voltage change.
Changed-task exit: infer an unknown voltage factor from an observed stored-energy ratio.
Repair the charge-versus-energy function: write Q ∝ V and U ∝ V² when C is fixed. Apply the factor once to Q and twice to U.
Fresh near re-entry: use a new voltage factor and new option structure with no exposed answer.
Repair the inverse inference: for fixed C, take the square root of the energy factor to recover the voltage factor.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: recover a voltage factor from a new fixed-capacitance energy factor without repeating the earlier values.
Recap: Q = CV; U = 1/2 CV² = 1/2 QV = Q²/(2C). Name the fixed quantity before comparing factors.
Starting check: classify a two-capacitor connection. A blank response records an abstention and grants no exit credit.

Goal: combine capacitors in series or parallel and predict a fully inserted dielectric’s effect under a stated battery condition. The packet declares no hard prerequisite, so topology and boundary conditions are taught explicitly.
Capacitors in parallel share both endpoint nodes and therefore share voltage; their capacitances add: Ceq = C1 + C2 + ….
Capacitors in series lie on one path and carry equal-magnitude charge in the ideal steady state; reciprocals add: 1/Ceq = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + …. The series equivalent is smaller than either member.
A dielectric that fully fills the gap increases capacitance to κC. If the battery remains connected, V stays fixed and Q increases. If the capacitor is isolated, Q stays fixed and V decreases.
Mental model: parallel adds storage width; series adds effective gap. A dielectric improves polarization support, but the external connection decides which electrical quantity can change.

Think aloud: two equal capacitors share both nodes, so they are parallel and give 2C. If instead they form one path, reciprocal addition gives C/2. Before analyzing a dielectric, I look for a connected battery: connected means fixed V; disconnected means fixed Q.
Worked example: C and 2C in parallel give 3C. The same pair in series gives Ceq = (C·2C)/(C + 2C) = 2C/3.
For an isolated charged capacitor, inserting a dielectric raises C while Q stays fixed; V = Q/C and U = Q²/(2C) both decrease.
Guided practice: mark endpoint nodes, select direct or reciprocal addition, then label the battery condition before predicting dielectric consequences.
Less support: use the bounds—parallel exceeds the largest member; series is below the smallest—to check a proposed equivalent.
On your own: calculate a fresh network and dielectric consequence without topology labels.
Boundary: physical side-by-side placement does not prove parallel connection; shared endpoint nodes do. A dielectric does not always raise stored energy: energy rises at fixed V but falls at fixed Q.
Near exit: calculate a mixed comparison between equal-capacitor series and parallel networks.
Changed-task exit: predict charge and energy after dielectric insertion using a stated battery connection.
Repair the network function: trace nodes first. Shared endpoints mean direct addition; one path means reciprocal addition. Check the result against the parallel-high and series-low bounds.
Fresh near re-entry: combine unequal capacitors in a new topology with new values.
Repair the dielectric function: write Cnew = κC, then lock V if connected or Q if isolated. Only then choose Q, V, and U changes.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: analyze the opposite battery condition with a new dielectric factor and no repeated answer.
Recap: parallel capacitances add; series reciprocals add; dielectrics raise C. The battery connection determines whether V or Q remains fixed.
